message:
feat(update): publish manifests, and make three runtimes agree on one signature

The manifest now has a publisher and three readers. What makes that worth
something is the shared vectors: C++, JavaScript and Kotlin each verify the
same fixed document, the same signature, the same key -- so the claim is that
three independent implementations accept one real artifact and reject the same
tampering, not that each agrees with itself.

Kotlin is where the representations diverge. JCA wants DER while the wire
carries raw r||s, because that is what CNG verifies on Windows. Converting in
Kotlin rather than changing the wire keeps one representation across all three,
and the test unwraps DER back to raw so the inverse runs too.

The server endpoint refuses more than it serves. It does not stream artifacts:
this process runs the relay and the heartbeat on the same event loop, and a
multi-megabyte installer would put every session on the box behind a download.
The manifest says where the artifact is, and something built for files serves
it. Authentication reuses the session or host token that already exists, since
an update check is something a signed-in machine does and a third credential is
a third thing to get wrong. The platform is whitelisted rather than sanitised,
because it becomes part of a filename and there are exactly two of them. With
REMOTE60_UPDATE_DIR unset the endpoint is simply off -- there is no default
directory to fall into. And when a public key is configured, the server reads
back what it is about to hand out: a manifest whose signature is wrong would
fail on every client, and the first to notice should not be a user.

Both JS and Kotlin ship with an empty trusted key, matching Windows. The Kotlin
test asserts that the empty key verifies nothing, so a placeholder cannot
appear quietly.

qwinsta: console active, rdp-tcp listening. JS 34 checks, Kotlin 9 tests,
server endpoint 16 checks, and the whole directory suite green. Nothing was
deployed; the server change is code only.
